narrative:
Tiananmen Square has been a central stage for major political movements in modern Chinese history, serving first as a venue for state-orchestrated mobilization and later for popular protest. Between August and November 1966, the square hosted eight Red Guard rallies under Mao and fellow ideologues that whipped up political hysteria during the Cultural Revolution [[1]]. More than a decade later, on November 27, 1978, the Democracy Wall movement brought tens of thousands to Tiananmen Square demanding democracy and human rights for China [[1]].

The most significant demonstrations began on April 15, 1989, triggered by the death of Hu Yaobang, after which university students began gathering in Tiananmen Square [[1]]. Over the following weeks, from April through June, tens of thousands of defiant students flooded into the streets and marched in a swelling parade toward the square, igniting a popular, nationwide movement demanding democracy, accountability, and freedom of speech [[1]]. The protests, which lasted over seven weeks, drew approximately a million participants who called for free speech, a free press, and less corruption [[2]]. Students were joined by a broad cross-section of Chinese society, and the demonstrations spread across the country [[3]]. The movement represented Chinese students seeking to build a better China, and according to one observer, "Our youth and intellectuals fell in love with America in Tiananmen Square" [[2]].

The protests ended violently on June 3-4, 1989, when the People's Liberation Army, given orders to clear the square "with extreme prejudice," opened fire on protesters, killing thousands [[1]][[3]]. The Tiananmen incident led to the collapse of the liberalizing trends of Chinese governance [[2]]. Even years later, the government does not allow discussion of the Tiananmen Square massacre in mainland China, with people knowing better than to talk about the events [[2]][[3]].
